extracted.intended_audience: aspiring romance novelists and writers who want to write in a commercial/Nora Roberts style
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing commercial romance novels modeled on Nora Roberts’ approach, covering plot structure, characterization, tropes, setting, style, and market conventions. Geared toward authors drafting full-length romance novels for general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance plot structure (three-act romance arc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Must include the basic romance beats: Boy meets girl; Boy loses girl; Boy gets girl back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states this as the core formula — how you use it is flexible, but those elements should be present. Treat it as the high-level skeleton for pacing and emotional trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character development (growth and change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your heroine and the hero must grow and change over the course of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should have issues to work through; no issues = a boring story. Include vulnerability and emotional depth so both characters change by the end. Three-dimensional characters are a must.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main-couple agency and strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Both members of the main couple should be strong individuals, not wishy-washy or permanently rescued/damsels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heroine needs to be able to take care of herself, may accept help but should later help or rescue the hero; the heroine often forces the hero out of his comfort zone. Avoid creating a hero who is only sulky/brooding or a heroine who lacks agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Show how each character’s past affects their present relationship and choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use backstory to explain motivations and emotional stakes — it should materially influence the relationship and plot rather than being decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstacles must be believable
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce plenty of believable obstacles to the budding relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obstacles provide conflict and force growth; they should feel grounded and plausible within the story world rather than contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sex scenes if you can’t write them well
rubrics_metrics.description: If sex scenes are not your forte, avoid them because poorly written erotic content will harm the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article bluntly advises writers inexperienced with sex scenes to steer clear rather than include weak or embarrassing passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cliché characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on over-done, stereotypical character types (e.g., sulky, brooding hero repeated across books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clichés make characters and stories feel stale; put fresh traits and complexity into familiar archetypes to keep readers engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tropes but put your own spin on them
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn common romance tropes (friends-to-lovers, enemies-to-lovers, healing arcs, second-chance romances) and make them your own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar tropes are acceptable and often expected; the key is to subvert, deepen, or personalize them so readers feel engaged and come back for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation must be clear and compelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters’ motivations must explain why they act — especially when actions push others away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make internal beliefs, fears, or past experiences drive choices so readers understand and empathize. Motivation is the reason a character chooses one course over another and is central to making tropes feel fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing style: polish, readability, and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: How you write matters: polish grammar, avoid clichés, balance pacing, and remove distracting dialogue tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recommends careful editing for readability and using tools (e.g., ProWritingAid) to find repeated phrases, improve word choice, and refine pacing. Strong line-level writing supports commercial romance sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitive phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeat the same descriptive phrases or adjectives across sentences/paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: repeatedly calling the hero 'classically handsome' becomes distracting. Use repetition reports or synonym tools to vary language and keep prose fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and/or define a niche (sub-genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which romance sub-genre you’re writing in (contemporary, historical, fantasy, paranormal, YA, religious, erotic, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planners should pick a niche early to guide worldbuilding and plot details; pantsters can write first and identify the niche later. Combining sub-genres is acceptable and often successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the setting prominent (setting as character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat setting nearly like a three-dimensional character; make it immersive and believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially important in historical or highly specific sub-genres — research thoroughly. Techniques include drawing maps, using hometown details, and selecting vivid, recurring locales to immerse readers (example: Outlander’s Scottish Highlands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver a satisfying (happy) ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance readers expect a happy ending — at minimum 'happy right now' even if not 'happily ever after.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t disappoint readers by leaving major threads dangling. Tie up important plotlines and character arcs unless leaving a deliberate, signaled hook for a sequel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve loose ends or justify sequels
rubrics_metrics.description: All major and relevant minor story threads should be wrapped up unless intentionally setting up a sequel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers dislike finding major unresolved threads. Minor character arcs can be left open only with clear intent for continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be confident about grammar (mechanics matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check and fix grammar mistakes before submitting or publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polished mechanics are expected; the article briefly urges writers to proofread and use grammar-checking tools to eliminate errors that distract readers.
